subject: Covariates increase AIC, but also significantly increases estimated N and graph "doesn't look right"

messages.author: cfb364282622bc71
messages.subject: Covariates increase AIC, but also significantly increases estimated N and graph "doesn't look right"
parts:
Hi All,

Quite often when I add a covariate (e.g. seastate, migration etc) in Rdistance, the hazard rate detection function sufficiently improves the AIC, but also significantly increases estimated N (sometimes by 1000’s from observations of only couple hundred). The resulting plotted detection probability also does not “look” good. It’s a steep decline, and bar starts at ~0.2 at zero distance (which then leads to a very low average detection probability – please find graph attached). Although the AIC suggests better fit, should this detection function be chosen? I remember reading in the Review paper of Distance by Thomas et al., 2010 that Hazard Rate model can often fit implausible shapes, especially for spiked data (which from exploratory analysis, I believe my data is). I am struggling to choose between a hazard rate model which has a much lower AIC but significantly increases estimated N (and has a much lower estimated PA) or a half normal model which has an AIC of at least 10 higher than HR, and seems to underestimate N. If anyone could shed any light on this, I would be very grateful.

 

Thanks,
Raph

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covariates increase AIC, but also significantly increases estimated N and graph "doesn't look right"
parts:
Raph

That's a good observation on your part, recognising that the hazard rate model, in some circumstances, produces large abundance estimates because of its rapid steep decline.  Out of curiosity, how many detections are in the data set you show?  We have seen this behaviour in the hazard rate model for small (<30) data sets.

AIC is used as a guide in model selection; it is not the only criterion to be used.  The analyst needs to also incorporate biological plausibility into their model selection decisions.  The figure you present suggests that average detectability is estimated to be ~0.2 at 100m (don't know units?).  In some circumstances that may be biologically plausible (ants in the jungle); in other situations (blue whales in the ocean) that may be quite unreasonable.  Without knowing more about the study that gave rise to the data, it is hard to say more.

Eric Rexstad

parts:
Hi Eric,

Thanks for your quick response. Looking through this forum has been very useful, with many of the previous questions and responses answering a lot of things that were on my mind!

In this particular example, the study was a set of line transects capturing distribution of whales, during different migration periods and over several years. For the model above, there were 57 observations in total after truncation. I decided to truncate at the 85th percentile but wasn't sure whether truncating even further would limit the model due to the (smallish) sample size already. What I have just noticed however, the graph above shows the detection function with ~as.factor(Migration) as a covariate - could it be that i am getting such a graph, because of the different amount of observations per migration (i.e. Northern migration may have 23 compared to southern migration with 34 observations and hence dataset is small).

Saying this, however, I get similar results with different years that have larger datasets (even when i have pooled all observations across all the years, my Hazard Rate detectability doesn't seem to get much bigger than 0.6 at 100m). One option is using a half normal, however the differences in estimated abundance between the two makes me question myself. 

Whilst we are on the subject of AIC and gof, I have noticed when I pool all years together, with more observations, many of my models have a CmV P value of less than 0.05 indicating no model fit. However, this may be due to the larger sample size (although still only~250 observations). So, is it then better to choose a model with a p-value that is above 0.05 or still be inclined with choosing the model with the lower AIC, even if it has a p value < 0.05 indicating no model fit? I hope this question makes sense.

Thanks for your time,

Raph
